title: Gut pulse scratch: candidate Ivy Cho
content:
Quick context
- Interview loop: senior runtime engineer (full loop + take-home)
- Candidate: Ivy Cho — senior backend/infra at mid-stage startup, led a small infra team (3-4) building inference pipelines
- Timeboxed: 90m loop + 24h take-home (matrix multiply batching exercise + KV cache sketch)

Immediate impressions (raw, unfiltered)
- Strong systems intuition but not deep ops-first: talks about failure modes with good mental models, but reached for org anecdotes rather than low-level kernel/driver details when probed.
- Code quality: take-home was tidy; prioritized readability and testability; missed an optimization that matters for long-tail batch cases (see notes below).
- Communication: concise, asks clarifying Qs early, surfaces assumptions quickly. Good collaborator vibe.
- Risk signal: limited production-scale GPU/attended tuning experience — said they had infra-level ownership but not HW-profiling/quant kernels.

Heuristic scorecard (quick, subjective) — 1 (low) to 5 (high)
- Algo/ML-ops intuition: 4
- Kernel/hardware tuning experience: 2
- Distributed systems: 4
- Debugging throughput/latency regressions: 3
- Ownership & shipping in small teams: 5
- Interview communication / mentoring fit: 4

Top positives
- Pragmatic tradeoff reasoning: balances latency/cost and explains why they would choose cache+small-model routing for certain SLOs.
- Ownership mindset: concrete examples of rollouts, incident postmortems they led, and how they changed monitoring thresholds.
- Clear pairing signal: would be pleasant to pair with product infra engineers — explains tradeoffs without being prescriptive.

Top concerns / open questions
- Limited hands-on kernel/quant experience: they haven't directly worked on CUDA kernels or post-training quantization pipelines beyond reading papers. For Redwood's runtime optimization focus this is notable.
- Scale exposure: most recent infra handled tens of nodes, not hundreds of GPU-cluster scheduling scenarios. Curious how they'd adapt to highly parallel KV cache pressure across many concurrent models.
- Take-home missed a pathological batching case: when sequences are heavy-tailed, their batching logic starves short-seq latency. I annotated the test. If candidate can reason through mitigation in follow-up, that would change the signal.

Questions to ask in follow-up (if we choose to move forward)
- Walk me through a concrete instance you optimized a production latency hotspot: tooling used, how you isolated root cause, and the quick vs permanent fixes.
- Have you ever instrumented a model runtime at token-level to find tail latency? Which traces/metrics did you find most actionable?
- Describe a time you had to trade off model quality for cost/latency — what metrics did you track to validate the decision?
- Would you be comfortable pairing to add a quantized code path to an existing runtime? What would be the first three things you check?

Take-home follow-up notes (what I annotated for reviewer):
- Test: add long-tail sequence simulation (many short sequences + a few very long ones) and measure P95/P99 latency; candidate's batching policy should adapt.
- Suggestion: ask candidate to sketch a fallback policy for cold KV cache misses (circuit-breaker + degraded-output mode) and how they'd measure safety.

Recommendation draft (leaning)
- Lean hire with a targeted growth plan: strong for cross-functional runtime/product work and incident ownership, but we should explicitly pair them with someone from runtime-engineering for a 2–3 week onboarding project focused on kernel/quant exposure.
- Compensation / level: strong senior (IC4) fit; lacks IC5 kernel depth today.

Next steps for interview ops
- If hiring committee wants stronger kernel signal -> schedule 1.5h deep-dive with serving-runtime engineer (Marcus suggested a focused CUDA/quant conversation).
- Else -> move to reference checks and discuss ramp plan with hiring manager (pairing project + internal mentor).

Notes to self (private heuristics)
- Candidate makes good engineering tradeoffs but will need structured upskilling on low-level kernels. Not a blocker if we accept mentorship model.
- Watch for language like "we relied on vendor X" — could indicate less internal ownership vs coordinating vendor integrations.

Quick copy for panel (one-paragraph):
Ivy Cho is a pragmatic senior infra engineer with solid distributed-systems instincts and strong ownership experience. The take-home was clean but missed an edge-case in batching for heavy-tailed sequences; candidate has the reasoning to close that gap but lacks direct kernel/quant experience. Recommend hire at senior level with a pairing-focused ramp or schedule a short kernel deep-dive if committee needs more signal.

Timestamp / logistical
- Drafted: 2024-11-03 22:10 PT
- Updated with take-home annotation and Marcus feedback: 2024-11-05 09:34 PT

Random crumbs (non-blocking)
- Slack snippet where candidate mentioned their infra blog: https://candidate-blog.example/ivy-cho-infra
- If we progress, ask recruiting to surface a sample of incidents Ivy led (postmortems) — high signal for ownership.
